notes: Proverbs teaches through compact sayings, extended speeches, questions, and images. Its sayings invite judgment about situations; the book also sets sayings beside one another that pull in different directions, as in 26:4–5.
The father addresses a son, and Wisdom speaks as a woman. These voices remain distinct. Wisdom’s laughter at disaster is part of her severe warning, not a softened narrator’s comment.
vocabulary: Fear of the LORD
Reverent fear that shapes how a person learns and acts; a recurring starting point for wisdom in this book.

sections.8: Do Not Join Those Who Shed Blood

notes: The “forbidden woman” is literally a strange or outsider woman. The companion and covenant language makes sexual unfaithfulness central; the wording does not require that she be ethnically foreign.
vocabulary: Shades of the dead
The Hebrew rephaim names the dead as inhabitants of the underworld.

sections.20: Walk in the Way of the Good

notes: “Body” renders the Hebrew “navel,” a bodily image paired with bones.
“Devastation of the wicked” can mean devastation that strikes them or comes from them. In verse 26 the LORD is “at your side,” or “your confidence.”

The precise precious material in verse 15 is uncertain. Verse 34 follows the read form “humble”; the written form is “poor.” Verse 35 has a difficult lifting verb: fools may carry away disgrace or raise it into prominence.
vocabulary: Tree of life
A life-giving tree image used for wisdom here, and for healing speech and fulfilled desire elsewhere in Proverbs.

notes: “The only one” describes the speaker’s place in his mother’s sight. Verse 7 can mean the beginning or the chief requirement of wisdom; its repeated command is to acquire wisdom and understanding.
Verse 16 follows the read form “make someone fall.” In verse 26 the verb can mean making a path level or weighing it carefully.
vocabulary: Heart
The inner center of thought, desire, and decision, not feelings alone.

sections.14: Do Not Enter the Path of the Wicked

notes: Verse 6 is read with the woman as subject, though some forms can address the son. Verse 16 is read as a question; the Hebrew can also be read as an assertion about springs spreading outside.
vocabulary: Cistern and fountain
Water sources become images of marital intimacy. The poem then speaks directly of the wife and her body.

sections.15: Rejoice in the Love of Your Marriage

notes: The first line is compressed: it may state a prostitute’s price as a loaf of bread, or say that involvement with her reduces someone to a loaf. The second line warns that adultery imperils a precious life.
vocabulary: Guarantee a debt
Accept responsibility for another person’s payment. The clasped hands mark a binding pledge.

sections.1: If You Have Pledged Yourself for Another

notes: The middle comparison in verse 22 is difficult. This draft retains the Hebrew’s fetters, correction, and fool rather than replacing them with another animal. The arrow pierces the liver in verse 23.
The last line can emphasize the great number or the strength of those killed. “A mighty host” retains both possibilities without specifying individuals.
vocabulary: Fellowship offerings
Sacrifices associated with a shared meal. The speaker invokes fulfilled vows while enticing the young man.

sections.10: She Came Out to Meet Him
sections.24: Do Not Wander into Her Ways

notes: “Acquired” renders qanah, which can express acquiring or possessing and can carry a creating sense. The poem next speaks of Wisdom being established and brought forth. This personified speech does not itself settle later theological debates.
“Master worker” renders the uncertain amon. Another reading pictures Wisdom as a child beside God; the following lines explicitly describe playing and delight.
vocabulary: Misses me
The verb can mean missing a mark or sinning. Here it contrasts finding Wisdom and life with harming oneself.

notes: Wisdom and Folly give the same invitation. The repeated wording asks the reader to distinguish their offerings and destinations.
“The Holy One” reads the plural Hebrew “holy ones” as a designation of God. A reference to holy beings is also possible.
vocabulary: Sheol
The realm of the dead, the destination hidden behind Folly’s invitation.

notes: “The mouth of the wicked conceals violence” can also be read “violence covers the mouth of the wicked.” Verse 22 may say God adds no sorrow to his blessing, or that toil adds nothing to it.
vocabulary: Discipline
Training that includes correction. The person who receives it can guide others; rejecting it can mislead them.

notes: Verse 16 contrasts a gracious woman’s honor with wealth held by ruthless men. In verse 30 “wins lives” is literally “takes lives,” a difficult expression here; the draft reads it positively with wisdom, without making it a technical term for conversion.
vocabulary: Accurate weight
A correctly sized stone used with balance scales; false weights enable commercial theft.

notes: Several compact clauses are difficult: verse 12 may refer to an evil catch, net, or stronghold; verse 26 to guiding or examining a neighbor; verse 27 to roasting game or obtaining it. Verse 28 retains the pinned text’s “no death.” These choices remain open for editorial review.
vocabulary: Capable
The Hebrew chayil includes strength, ability, and worth; it reappears prominently in 31:10–31.

notes: Wealth “from emptiness” may be insubstantial or dishonestly obtained wealth. The “hard” way in verse 15 uses a word that can also mean enduring or firm; the contrast favors difficulty here.
The first saying names injustice that takes the poor’s food. The next retains a rod in parental discipline; the physical image has not been replaced with a general term for teaching.
vocabulary: Tree of life
An image for the restoring force of a desire fulfilled, contrasting a sick heart.

notes: Verse 9 may concern guilt or a guilt offering. Verse 14 leaves the good person’s return compressed; the draft supplies deeds in parallel with ways. “His children” in verse 26 has an uncertain possessor. Verse 33 retains the affirmative statement that wisdom is known even among fools.
vocabulary: Maker
The Creator of the poor person; treatment of that person is presented as treatment of the Maker.

notes: The widow’s boundary is a property boundary. The contrast concerns both the proud person’s house and a vulnerable person’s protected land.
vocabulary: Abaddon
“Destruction,” paired with Sheol as a name for the realm of the dead.

sections.16: Better with the Fear of the LORD

notes: The poem attributes purpose even to the wicked’s day of disaster. Verse 6 does not specify whose faithful love and faithfulness atone for guilt. Verse 10 is rendered as a royal obligation to judge faithfully, not a claim that every king always does so.
vocabulary: Roll your works onto the LORD
A concrete image for entrusting one’s undertakings to God.

sections.26: The Power of Speech and Self-Control

notes: The bribe’s apparent power is described from its owner’s viewpoint. The high doorway in verse 19 may suggest proud display, but the image is retained. Verse 27 follows the read form “noble/precious spirit”; the written form is “cool spirit.”
vocabulary: Pledge
A binding undertaking to pay another person’s debt, symbolized by clasped hands.

sections.1: Better a Dry Morsel with Peace

notes: “Harder to win” supplies the comparison implied in verse 19. The first line of verse 24 is difficult; this draft reads it as the danger of many companions, contrasted with one deeply loyal friend.
vocabulary: Lots
Objects cast to settle a decision; the saying describes their use in ending disputes.

sections.20: Life and Death in the Tongue

notes: The last clause is uncertain. This draft follows the written negative “not”; the read form is “to him.” The verse’s clear setting is the poor man’s abandonment, but the precise final wording remains difficult.

Verse 16 follows the read form “will die,” rather than the written “will be put to death.” Verse 18 explicitly warns against setting one’s heart on a son’s death. Verse 27 is read as an ironic warning about what follows if listening stops.
vocabulary: Lends to the LORD
An economic image that connects mercy toward the poor with God’s own repayment.

notes: Verse 16 follows the read form referring to an outsider woman; the written form refers to outsiders in the plural. Verse 21 follows “hastily acquired.” Verse 30 retains wounding blows and follows the read form’s cleansing expression.
vocabulary: Holy
Set apart for God. The warning concerns making a vow before considering its cost.

notes: “Lamp” in verse 4 can also be understood as a plowed field. Verse 6 follows the pinned “seekers of death,” rather than “snares of death.” Verse 12 reads “the Righteous One” as God; a righteous human observer is also possible.
vocabulary: Ransom
Something given in another’s place. Here the image describes a reversal between the wicked and the righteous.

notes: Verse 4 can link humility and fear as two qualities or make fear follow humility. Verse 6 says “according to his way,” leaving the precise relation of training and the youth’s way open. Verse 16 compresses the relationship between oppression, gain, giving, and poverty.

The written form can mean “formerly.” The read form is understood here as “excellent sayings”; another interpretation yields “thirty sayings.” The draft does not impose a numbered scheme on the following units.
vocabulary: Gate
The city’s public place for legal and civic business; crushing the poor there includes denying justice.

notes: The knife at the throat is a forceful image of appetite restrained. Verses 13–14 explicitly describe striking a youth with a rod and its claimed protective purpose; the translation preserves that ancient disciplinary language.
“Innermost being” is literally “kidneys.” Verse 26 follows the read form “keep/watch,” not the written “delight.” “Strange things” in verse 33 can also be understood as strange women.
vocabulary: Redeemer
A defender who takes up another’s cause, drawing on the role of a family protector.

sections.1: Do Not Exhaust Yourself for Wealth
sections.22: Buy Truth and Do Not Sell It
sections.29: Do Not Be Captivated by Wine

notes: The warning forbids delight in an enemy’s downfall. In verse 22 “both” most naturally points back to the LORD and the king; the compressed pronouns should not be made into an extra threat against the reader.
vocabulary: Seven times
A repeated, full measure of falling and rising; the context concerns adversity rather than naming seven particular sins.

sections.1: By Wisdom a House Is Built
sections.11: Rescue Those Being Taken to Death

notes: The clause “what your eyes have seen” is kept in verse 7 but read with verse 8. The coals on an enemy’s head in verse 22 are not explained in the proverb; shame, changed relations, and judgment are interpretive possibilities.

The second line is unusually compressed and contains no explicit negative. It can be read as “searching out their glory is glory,” with the word’s related sense of weight. The draft carries the first line’s negation forward and reads a warning against pursuing one’s own honor. That negative is implied rather than written; the positive reading remains a serious alternative.
vocabulary: Soda
A mineral cleaning substance, not a modern soft drink. Vinegar disrupts it, matching the ill-timed song.

sections.1: Proverbs Copied in the Days of Hezekiah

notes: Verse 2 follows the written “not”; the read form is “to him,” which can suggest a curse returning to its source. Verses 4–5 deliberately give opposite instructions with different consequences. Both are retained for discernment, not merged into one rule.

Verse 10 is exceptionally difficult; “archer” and “wounds” are selected, but readings involving a master or great person are possible. Verse 23 retains the pinned silver dross and burning lips, rather than silently substituting smooth lips.
vocabulary: Whisperer
A person whose private talk spreads suspicion or gossip; the morsel image shows its appeal.

notes: These sayings are compressed. Verse 9 connects friendship’s sweetness with heartfelt counsel. Verse 16’s final verb is uncertain; the draft uses the image of grasping oil. Verse 19 leaves the heart’s reflection broad. “His praise” in verse 21 can concern praise received or what someone praises.
vocabulary: Flock and herds
Living sources of clothing, exchange, and food, contrasted with wealth and status that may not endure.

sections.22: Know the Condition of Your Flocks

notes: Verse 3 retains “poor man” as the oppressor. Verse 14 describes continual fear without naming its object; “reverent” reads it in the book’s wisdom setting. Verse 18 may mean falling suddenly or falling in one of the crooked ways.
vocabulary: Instruction
Torah: authoritative teaching that is heard and kept. Here it is the measure of conduct and even of prayer.

notes: Verse 10’s “seek his life” is read as protective care by the upright; the syntax is difficult. The rare word manon in verse 21 is read as son-like status, but its exact meaning is uncertain.
vocabulary: Prophetic vision
Revelatory guidance, not simply a personal ambition or an organization’s plan.

notes: The opening retains Ithiel and Ucal as names. Different word divisions can yield a declaration of weariness to God. “Oracle” may instead be the place-name Massa. “Holy One” in verse 3 represents a plural form. The son in verse 4 is left unidentified.

Verse 28 may describe a lizard grasping with its hands or being caught by hands. The animal in verse 31 is literally “girded at the loins”; rooster is a possible identification. The final phrase about the king’s company is also uncertain.
vocabulary: Pressing
One repeated Hebrew word connects milk, nose, and anger. “Nose” and “anger” are also related Hebrew expressions.

sections.4: Every Word of God Is Refined
sections.7: Give Me Neither Poverty nor Riches
sections.21: Four Things the Earth Cannot Bear

notes: “Oracle” may instead identify Massa. Those “passing away” in verse 8 can be understood as people facing ruin or destitution; the king is told to defend their rights.
The twenty-two verses form a Hebrew alphabetic poem, one successive letter at the start of each verse. It praises a woman’s strength, productive work, generosity, teaching, and public standing.

The young women’s allotment may mean provisions or assigned work. Verse 21 retains the pinned “scarlet,” rather than the alternative “double garments.” “Merchant” in verse 24 is literally “Canaanite,” used in a trading sense.
vocabulary: Strength
Chayil includes ability, resources, worth, and strength. The poem describes these in action rather than narrowing the word to one virtue.
